title: Finding the Main Idea
subject: ELA
developmentNotes: Third graders often confuse topic with main idea. Use short passages and evidence sorting before asking for written summaries.
learningObjective: Students will distinguish topic from main idea and support a main idea with key details from a short informational text.
essentialQuestion: How do readers figure out what a text is mostly teaching?

vocabularyTerms.definition: who or what the text is mostly about
the most important point the author wants you to understand
an important fact that supports the main idea
a short retelling of the most important ideas

prerequisites: Retell a short passage in order

hook.content: Students see three details: “They have roots,” “They need sunlight,” “They grow from seeds.” They decide what these details are mostly about and what main idea they support.
hook.studentAction: Predict, notice, or explain initial thinking before direct instruction.
hook.teacherOrAppAction: Capture initial response as non-graded diagnostic evidence.

learningGoal.content: I can students will distinguish topic from main idea and support a main idea with key details from a short informational text.
successCriteria: I can explain the core concept in my own words.
I can show evidence or reasoning, not only an answer.
I can correct a common mistake.

miniTeach.content: The topic is the subject. The main idea is the important message about that subject. Details are pieces of evidence that prove the main idea. If the topic is plants, the main idea might be “Plants need several things to grow.”
miniTeach.cognitiveLoadNotes: Use short chunks, one example at a time, and reveal labels only after students observe the model.

firstPrinciplesBreakdown.coreConcept: Main idea is built from details.
known: Some details are more important than others.
A main idea must match most of the important details.
rules: A topic is usually a word or phrase.
A main idea is usually a full sentence.
Key details must support the main idea.
avoid: Do not choose a tiny detail as the main idea.
Do not choose an idea that only matches one sentence.
Do not confuse “plants” with “plants need water, sunlight, and soil to grow.”
steps: Ask: What do these details prove together?
Check that each key detail supports it.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.check: If a detail does not support the main idea, revise the main idea or choose stronger evidence.

workedExample.content: Passage: “Bees visit flowers to collect nectar. As bees move, pollen sticks to their bodies. When they land on another flower, the pollen can help the plant make seeds.” Topic: bees and flowers. Main idea: Bees help many plants make seeds. Key details: bees collect nectar, pollen sticks, pollen moves to another flower.
workedExample.teacherOrAppAction: Highlight each reasoning step and connect it to the first-principles breakdown.

items: Sort cards into topic, main idea, and detail.
Choose the best main idea for a paragraph about frogs.
Cross out one detail that is interesting but not key.
Explain why “bees” is a topic but not a complete main idea.
guidedPractice.scaffolding: Start with high support, then remove hints. Require explanation on the final item.

criticalThinkingCheckpoint.prompt: Two students choose different main ideas. One matches all three key details; one matches only the first detail. Which is stronger and why?
criticalThinkingCheckpoint.lookFor: Student identifies assumption, evaluates reasoning, and explains why one answer or model is stronger.

evidenceBasedReasoningTask.prompt: Claim: The paragraph is mostly about how bees help plants. Choose two details from the text that prove the claim and explain how they support it.

interpretationOrDiscussionTask.prompt: Interpret the author’s purpose: Is the author trying to entertain, explain, or persuade? What clues show that?
interpretationOrDiscussionTask.safety: Use private response or moderated classroom mode only. No unrestricted student chat.

activePractice.content: Students highlight details in a paragraph, drag them into “supports main idea” or “extra detail,” then write one main idea sentence.

rules: Correct: explain why it works, not only mark correct.

reteachPath.misconception: Student confuses a topic or interesting detail with the main idea.
reteachPath.simpleExplanation: A topic names the subject. A main idea says the big point about that subject.
steps: Ask what the paragraph is mostly about.
Ask what the details have in common.
Check each detail against the sentence.

practice.prompt: Topic or main idea: “Sharks have special body parts that help them hunt.”
Choose a key detail for “Plants need care.”
Fix: Main idea = “sunlight” for a plant-growth passage
practice.answer: Plants need sunlight, water, and soil to grow.

reteachPath.exitCriteria: Student completes at least 4 of 5 reteach items and explains the corrected misconception.

tasks: Compare two possible main ideas and rank which one is more precise.
Write a 3-sentence summary using one main idea and two key details.
Find a detail that does not belong and explain why it weakens the summary.

parentTeacherNotes: Ask the student after reading nonfiction: “What was this mostly teaching? Which two details prove it?”
accessibilityNotes: Use plain, grade-appropriate language and define academic vocabulary before using it in prompts.
Provide alt text or text-equivalent descriptions for every image, diagram, array, chart, map, or model.
Make all interactive elements keyboard accessible with visible focus states and screen-reader labels.
Never rely only on color to communicate correct/incorrect, categories, or importance.
Provide read-aloud support for Foundation Academy and optional read-aloud for all grade bands.
Chunk instructions into short steps and provide examples before independent work.
safetyNotes: No public student posting, random direct messages, or unrestricted discussion.
Discussion prompts must use sentence frames and moderation/teacher controls when implemented.
Student-generated work should be visible only to the student and authorized parent/teacher roles unless explicitly assigned in a safe classroom workflow.
Do not collect unnecessary personal information in lesson responses.
implementationNotes: Render lessonFlow sections in order with progress state.
Persist quiz attempts and item-level skill tags.
Generate Memory Vault records after lesson completion.
Use mastery bands to branch to reteach, guided practice, review, or challenge.
Store open responses privately with role-based access.
Use answer keys and rubrics for review; do not expose hidden answer keys in student mode.
